newsitem.title: USA: Good government essential for growth --World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Good government essential for growth --World Bank.

text.p: Good government, based on sound laws and a stable economy, is an essential precondition for economic growth, according to a World Bank report released on Wednesday.

The report, arguing against a full laissez-faire economy, said an effective state had made possible the "dazzling growth" of the tiger economies of East Asia, where the government worked with businesses rather than against them.
"The message is not big government or small government, but that an effective state is vital for development," Ajay Chhibber, one of the authors of the 265-page document, told a news conference.
He said a country's institutional environment was, along with economic and social policies, important in determining whether an economy grew and how fast the growth rate was.
The World Bank survey, entitled "The State in a Changing World," did not single out countries by name.

But it noted that the credibility of the state was lowest in the former Soviet republics making up the Commonwealth of Independent States and greatest in the high-income members of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
"In order for us to gather data, we had to say we would not publish it from individual countries," said Joseph Stiglitz, the World Bank's Chief Economist.
He said World Bank officials surveyed 3,600 firms in 69 countries to collect data for their report, which also highlights the problems caused by corrupt officials and by crime and lawlessness.

The officials said some tasks had to be carried out by the state, including providing a functioning legal system, creating the framework for macro-economic stability, investing in social services and protecting the environment.
The state also needed to provide the framework to regulate markets and to win the confidence of its citizens, but it did not have to be the sole provider of services.
"Where governments lack the ways to listen, they are not responsive to peoples' interests, especially those of minorities and the poor," Chhibber said.
But it was not clear to what extent the report will influence future World Bank loan policy.

The bank, a sister organisation to the International Monetary Fund, tracks whether its own funds are used in a corrupt way, but does not make loans conditional on such things as a country meeting criteria on official corruption.
